title: Poke
description: One still frame of a tree against a summer sky, from a clip filmed on a tripod in the wind. Twenty-six seconds of its real motion were taken apart into the tree's own vibration modes: twelve shapes, each with the frequency and damping the clip measured, from a slow 0.36 Hz sway of the whole crown to quicker 1.3 Hz shivers in single branches. Nothing is shown as a photograph: the whole print is one line engraving on a cobalt-shadow ground. The crown's lines are cut along the contours of the leaves' light, each one swelling where the leaves are lit; the sky is ruled with finer, nearly level lines that thin toward the top and swell and crowd together where a cloud brightens, and the two hatchings stop against each other where they meet. Take hold of any part of the tree and pull. The whole crown answers through the modes it shares with that spot, each part with its own lag, and its lines bend with it where it shears and keep their light, their trailing ends drawing out a little, against a sky whose ruling holds still and carries on behind wherever the crown swings away. Their colour turns with where each part is in its swing: gold with your hand, violet against it, teal as it leads, rose as it lags, or either as it swings aside, deeper the harder it moves. Let go and everything rings down in its own time, coupled the way the real branches are. Nothing about the motion is invented.
intent: Image-Space Modal Bases / Interactive Dynamic Video: Abe Davis, Justin G. Chen and Fredo Durand, 'Image-Space Modal Bases for Plausible Manipulation of Objects in Video', ACM Transactions on Graphics 34(6), SIGGRAPH Asia 2015 (https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/137568, https://www.provideocoalition.com/pokemon-go-interactive-dynamic-video/), the method that Generative Image Dynamics (Li, Tucker, Snavely and Holynski, CVPR 2024) drives with a diffusion prior. Here it runs on real footage, as in the original. Offline (tools/depth/bakes/poke): DIS optical flow from a reference frame to all 772 frames, photometrically checked; Frequency Domain Decomposition (Brincker, Zhang and Andersen 2000) of all the motion at once, so every singular vector at a spectral peak is a complex 2D mode shape; the twelve strongest spatially coherent ones kept; frequency and damping from an SDOF fit to each modal coordinate's spectrum; quantised into a 12-layer texture array. Live: complex modal oscillators driven by the hand, a closed-loop spring over a hand-sized patch of the crown (the Gaussian-weighted mean shape, so incoherent shivers inside it cancel) whose force is projected onto the modes (f_i = phi_i(m)^H F). The unit-norm shapes leave relative modal mass free, so they are tilted by (f0/f)^2 toward the slow crown-wide modes, which makes a pull swing the whole crown rather than one clump. The tree is matted off a filled, regraded sky, and no photograph is drawn: the print is rendered only as a line engraving on a cobalt-shadow ground. Its lines are evenly spaced streamlines (Jobard and Lefer 1997) of the contour direction of the light (the smoothed structure tensor of its gradient), seeded in shuffled jittered order and outward from each finished line, cut into strokes of varied length; each stroke is an instanced ribbon whose width at every spine point is the light there. The crown's follow the leaves' luminance, with a hairline floor in deep shadow. The sky's follow its own softened luminance at the same pitch, with a far broader smoothing and a strong level bias, so they run nearly horizontally and drift with the polariser falloff; they are finer and in a cool pale ink, and their separation closes up where a cloud brightens, so a cloud is lines swelling and bunching. Both hatchings are laid into one separation grid, the crown first, so the sky's lines terminate against the crown's by the same separation test. Each sky line that stops at the crown runs on beneath it, and a cover map of the crown's lines (drawn wide, at rest and as they are now) hides the sky's ruling where the crown swings over it and shows that hidden continuation where it swings away. Every crown spine point is carried by the modal field at its own rest position, so a pull bends the strokes where the crown shears; each ribbon keeps the width of the leaves' light at its rest position, and only an end that trails its motion lags, by a share of its displacement capped at one and a half line pitches, so the engraving's lit clumps and shadows survive a full pull. The crown's streamlines must run at least eight separations to be laid and are cut into strokes of 14 to 36, so they run long and bunch into moire where the contours converge. Each crown stroke's OKLCH lightness is the leaves' light at its rest position, near-white cream in the lit clumps falling to a dark hairline ink in shadow, whatever the pull. Only its hue is the angle of the analytic signal sum_i phi_i (q_i - i v_i / omega_i) in the frame of the pull (gold with the hand, violet against it, teal leading, rose lagging, either one swinging aside), at a chroma capped near 0.075 and scaled by light times amplitude (easing off again in the brightest light), so a frozen still shows the twelve-mode structure as a cool/warm cast running through an intact engraving rather than a colour map. Developed through the lab film kit (summer). Patent note: MIT holds a patent on this method (Davis et al., image-space modal bases / interactive dynamic video). This is a non-commercial portfolio reimplementation of the published paper; clear it before any commercial use. Stills: ?poke=x,y,amp[,deg]&t=seconds (print uv, pull as a fraction of the print's width toward deg, default left; t after letting go, omit to hold), ?still=1 stops the breeze.

sources.author: Engin Akyurt (https://www.pexels.com/@enginakyurt/)
sources.note: 1920x1080, 29.97 fps, 25.8 s, locked off on a tripod. Reference frame 382 (the frame closest to the clip's mean pose). Flow with OpenCV DIS at 960x540, modal grid 320x180. Tree matted off the sky by colour and a guided filter; sky behind filled by push-pull and regraded toward the genre's cobalt (polariser-like, deeper at the top).
